title: We All Need Microadventures
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: Katherine Martinko introduces Alastair Humphreys's idea of the microadventure, a short, simple, local and cheap outing meant to counter urban, screen-bound routines. She agrees with his diagnosis that screen addiction is worse now than when he began promoting the idea in 2015, but disagrees with his requirement to sleep outdoors, fearing it will intimidate families. She proposes a broader definition: any activity of at least two hours that involves leaving home or property, ideally outdoors. She offers examples from readers and her own family life, including seeking water, wandering with a dog, picnic meals, fires with her kids, snowshoeing, stargazing and motorcycle rides to meet friends. Her point is that such outings break routine, clear screen-induced cobwebs and leave people refreshed.
points: Humphreys's microadventure reframes the hours between work and bed as a realistic window for adventure rather than treating the job as the obstacle.
Martinko drops the overnight requirement and defines a microadventure as any outing of at least two hours that leaves the house, so more families will actually try it.
Small, repeatable family rituals such as picnic dinners, backyard-adjacent fires, snowshoe cookouts and meteor-shower nights make the outdoors part of weekday life.
The purpose is to counteract screen-induced stagnation by getting outside, breathing fresh air and recovering wonder at the natural world.
quotes: Rather than view our 9-to-5 jobs as an obstacle to adventure, we should view the remaining 16 hours between 5 PM and 9 AM as an opportunity to do something fun and outdoorsy, that breaks us out of routine and makes us feel like we’re squeezing more out of our lives.
A person does not need to consider themselves an adventurer to go on a microadventure; they simply have to leave their house and see what happens.
His message is more important than ever, with our collective screen addiction arguably far worse now than it was in 2015, when he first started talking about this idea.

So, I would suggest a broader interpretation of the microadventure to include any sort of activity, ideally outdoors but not necessarily, that lasts a minimum of two hours and involves leaving one’s home or property.
Picnic dinners and breakfasts are another lovely way to get families outside on weekdays. The food itself doesn’t have to be fancy; the novel setting makes it special.
I also like building fires with my kids, which would be an exception to the “leave your property” rule. It gives them something to do, to tend and then gather round.

Whatever you choose to do, the point of a microadventure is to snap us out of routine and banish the screen-induced cobwebs from our brains by getting outside, breathing fresh air, and reminding ourselves of just how wondrous the natural world is.
